title: Message Type Indicators (MTIs)

blocks.text: Every ISO-8583 message opens with four digits, and those four digits are the whole of its identity. Section 2.1 calls them the Message Type Indicator, and each one answers a different question: which edition of the standard the message is written against, what class of business it is, where in the exchange it sits, and which side of the link sent it.

The tables are short enough to hold in your head. A `0100` is an authorization request from an acquirer, written against the 1987 edition (version digit `0`; `1` is the 1993 edition and `2` the 2003 one). Change the third digit to a `1` and it becomes the response. Change the second to an `8` and the message is no longer about money at all — it is network management between the two ends of the link: sign-on, sign-off, key exchange, or an echo test that checks the link is alive.
That is the point of this first practice: an MTI is not opaque, and you do not need a library to read one.

Make `parts` in `practice/mti/Mti.java` return the four parts of an MTI — its version, its message class, its message function and its message origin, in that order — and refuse anything that is not four digits.
Lesson: a practice whose grader already passes

The file ships finished, so its grader passes the moment you press Submit. That is deliberate: the first thing worth knowing about a practice is what a green run looks like, and you cannot recognise a broken one until you have seen a working one. Press Run to see the file's own output, then Submit to see the grader's.
Then break it on purpose. Delete a case from `messageClass`, submit again, and read what the grader says. Put it back.
